searchDocs.title: When Reqsign fits​
searchDocs.content: You own the HTTP layer and want to keep it: a database's storage backend, a CLI, a gateway, an SDK of your own. You need wire-correct signatures, production-grade credential chains, and perhaps presigning or downscoped grants — without inheriting a vendor SDK's HTTP stack, retry policy, and dependency tree per cloud.

searchDocs.title: When a vendor SDK fits​
searchDocs.content: You need broad coverage of one cloud's API surface — management operations, typed request/response models, service-specific helpers — and the SDK's bundled stack fits your application. Signing is a fraction of what those SDKs do; Reqsign replaces only that fraction.

searchDocs.title: Relationship to Apache OpenDAL​
searchDocs.content: Reqsign started inside Apache OpenDAL™ and graduated to a standalone Apache top-level project in 2026. The two remain close, and the dependency points one way: OpenDAL's cloud storage services sign their requests with Reqsign; Reqsign does not depend on OpenDAL.  The two serve different builders. Reqsign gives you signing primitives for a client you are writing yourself. OpenDAL is a ready-made data access layer — if what you actually want is to read and write storage behind one API rather than construct requests, use OpenDAL and you get Reqsign's signing underneath for free.

searchDocs.title: Signer​
searchDocs.content: Signer composes the three pieces and adds a credential cache:  use reqsign::Signer; let signer = Signer::new(ctx, credential_provider, request_signer); signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;   Each sign call: checks the cached credential (still valid, and usable until the operation's deadline?); asks the provider for a fresh one if not; then hands the request head and credential to the request signer, which mutates req in place.  The exact behavior of sign — wire-ready URI ownership, atomicity on error,expires_in semantics — is contractual; seeSigning contracts.  Builders swap any component while keeping the others:  let signer = signer .with_context(custom_ctx) // clears the credential cache .with_credential_provider(static_provider) // clears the credential cache .with_request_signer(other_signer);

searchDocs.title: Context​
searchDocs.content: Context answers "where does I/O come from?" Credential providers need to read files, call metadata endpoints, inspect environment variables, and sometimes run CLIs — but Reqsign never hard-codes how. Every capability is a trait slot:  Capability	Trait	Default (default-context)Read files	FileRead	TokioFileRead Send HTTP requests	HttpSend	ReqwestHttpSend Read environment	Env	OsEnv Execute commands	CommandExecute	TokioCommandExecute  Context::new() wires no-op stubs, not silent fallbacks: a credential source that needs HTTP against a stub context returns an error instead of quietly doing nothing, so you always know which capabilities you granted. The facade's default_context() returns the full assembly in the table.  use reqsign::aws::{DefaultCredentialProvider, RequestSigner}; use reqsign::{Context, OsEnv, Signer}; use reqsign_command_execute_tokio::TokioCommandExecute; use reqsign_file_read_tokio::TokioFileRead; use reqsign_http_send_reqwest::ReqwestHttpSend; fn main() { let ctx = Context::new() .with_crypto(reqsign::RustCryptoProvider::new()) .with_file_read(TokioFileRead) .with_http_send(ReqwestHttpSend::default()) .with_env(OsEnv) .with_command_execute(TokioCommandExecute); let _signer = Signer::new( ctx, DefaultCredentialProvider::new(), RequestSigner::new("s3", "us-east-1"), ); }   This explicit assembly also needs reqsign-file-read-tokio,reqsign-command-execute-tokio, and reqsign-http-send-reqwest as direct dependencies; default_context() supplies the same components through the facade.  Why traits instead of feature flags: tests inject static env maps and canned HTTP responses without process-global mutation; sandboxes withhold capabilities by simply not providing them; and WASM targets provide browser-backed implementations. SeeCustom runtimes & WASM.

searchDocs.title: Crypto provider​
searchDocs.content: Cryptography is resolved through Context. Every hash, MAC, asymmetric signature, AES-GCM operation, and random draw callsctx.crypto_provider(), which prefers an explicitContext::with_crypto binding, then the process-wide provider installed withRustCryptoProvider::install_default():  use reqsign::{Context, RustCryptoProvider, Signer}; // Explicit provider for this context. let ctx = Context::new().with_crypto(RustCryptoProvider::new()); // Or install before constructing facade contexts to select one provider. RustCryptoProvider::install_default() .map_err(|_| "a CryptoProvider is already installed")?;   reqsign-core and the service crates contain no cryptographic implementation. A bare Context::new() starts unbound and returns ConfigInvalid when signing needs crypto without a global provider. The facade's default-crypto feature makes default_context() bind RustCrypto only when the process-wide slot is empty at construction; it never writes the slot. A context that already binds RustCrypto keeps it, and an explicit with_crypto binding always wins. Applications choose the provider, and integrating middleware such as OpenDAL must not install a global default. SeeCryptoProviderfor the full contract and error semantics.

searchDocs.title: ProvideCredential​
searchDocs.content: One trait behind every credential source — an env reader, a config-file parser, an IMDS client, an OIDC exchanger:  pub trait ProvideCredential { type Credential; async fn provide_credential(&self, ctx: &Context) -> Result<Option<Self::Credential>>; }   The Option is the chain protocol:  Ok(Some(credential)) — this source resolved a credential; use it.Ok(None) — this source has nothing to offer (env var unset, file missing); try the next source.Err(e) — this source failed (malformed file, network error). A directly installed provider propagates this error to the signer.  ProvideCredentialChain logs errors and continues to the next provider, just as it does for None. It returns Ok(None) when no provider succeeds. Do not use this chain when a source failure must prevent fallback to another identity.  Chains compose providers in order and take the first Some; because "not configured" is None rather than an error, a chain of ten sources stays quiet until one applies.  type Credential is deliberately not a universal struct: AWS needs an access key pair plus optional session token; Azure models SharedKey,SasToken, and BearerToken as an enum. Each service crate defines the credential its signer consumes, and the type system keeps mismatches impossible. Working with chains and writing your own provider:Loading credentials.

searchDocs.title: SignRequest​
searchDocs.content: SignRequest implements a provider's wire protocol: given a request head and a credential, produce that provider's exact authentication format.  pub trait SignRequest { type Credential; fn required_valid_until( &self, credential: &Self::Credential, expires_in: Option<Duration>, ) -> Timestamp; async fn sign_request( &self, ctx: &Context, req: &mut http::request::Parts, credential: Option<&Self::Credential>, expires_in: Option<Duration>, ) -> Result<()>; }   reqsign_aws_v4::RequestSigner produces SigV4's canonical request andAuthorization header — or X-Amz-* query parameters when expires_in is set. reqsign_azure_storage::RequestSigner produces Shared Key headers or appends a SAS token. The trait is shared; the wire behavior deliberately is not.  required_valid_until is how signing stays ahead of expiration: before signing, the signer asks how long the credential must remain usable — "now" for a header signature, the full window for a presigned URL — and refreshes a cached credential that cannot cover it.

searchDocs.title: Credential caching and validity​
searchDocs.content: Credential loading can be expensive (an IMDS round-trip, an OIDC exchange), so Signer and Granter cache what they load. Two methods onSigningCredential govern reuse:  pub trait SigningCredential { /// May a cached credential be reused? Implementations may include a /// proactive refresh window. fn is_valid(&self) -> bool; /// Is the credential usable at this exact timestamp? No buffers. fn is_valid_at(&self, ts: Timestamp) -> bool; }   The two checks have different jobs: is_valid answers the cachingquestion (refresh early rather than mid-flight); is_valid_at answers theoperation question against a deadline (a credential fine for header signing can be insufficient for a one-hour presign window). Both must reject credentials lacking the fields required for authentication.  The reuse rule on every sign or grant:  A cached credential is reused only if is_valid() and it satisfies the operation's deadline.Otherwise the provider is asked for a fresh credential, which only needs to satisfy the exact deadline.Errors returned by the configured provider are propagated without retry or reuse of the previous cached credential. A configured provider chain can handle errors internally by trying its next source, as described above.  Replacing a signer's or granter's context or credential provider clears the cache: a credential loaded under one configuration is never reused under another.

searchDocs.title: Granter and GrantCredential​
searchDocs.content: Signing proves a request is yours; granting gets you a narrower credential first. Providers each have an operation for this (S3 Access Grants, S3 Express CreateSession, Azure user delegation SAS, GCP Credential Access Boundary); Reqsign unifies their shape without hiding their semantics:  pub trait GrantCredential { type Credential: SigningCredential; fn required_valid_until( &self, credential: &Self::Credential, expires_in: Option<Duration>, ) -> Timestamp; async fn grant_credential( &self, ctx: &Context, credential: &Self::Credential, expires_in: Option<Duration>, ) -> Result<Self::Credential>; }   use reqsign::Granter; let granter = Granter::new(ctx, source_provider, granting_operation); let scoped = granter.grant(Some(Duration::from_secs(900))).await?;   Granter caches the source credential with the same rules as Signer, and a granted result owns independent material — it never aliases the cached source, so using it after the source rotates is safe. The walkthrough lives in Granting scoped access.

searchDocs.title: Compiles everywhere: dyn pairs and MaybeSend​
searchDocs.content: Two mechanics keep this composition model portable:  Every async trait Foo has a FooDyn counterpart with a blanket implementation, so Signer stores Arc<dyn FooDyn> internally while you implement the ergonomic non-dyn trait.Trait futures are MaybeSend: Send on native targets, relaxed onwasm32-unknown-unknown, which is why the crate compiles for the browser without an async_trait dependency.

searchDocs.title: Where to plug in​
searchDocs.content: The same components are reachable at three levels — pick by how much you want to control:  The facade (reqsign crate) — one dependency, feature flags per provider, default_context() for the standard runtime, and default_signerentries that wire each provider's credential chain and request signer with your supplied Context. Best for applications; still customizable throughwith_* builders.  Custom assembly — the same components, wired explicitly. Whatdefault_signer does for you, written out:  use reqsign::aws::{DefaultCredentialProvider, RequestSigner}; use reqsign::{Context, OsEnv, Signer}; use reqsign_command_execute_tokio::TokioCommandExecute; use reqsign_file_read_tokio::TokioFileRead; use reqsign_http_send_reqwest::ReqwestHttpSend; fn main() { let ctx = Context::new() .with_crypto(reqsign::RustCryptoProvider::new()) .with_file_read(TokioFileRead) .with_http_send(ReqwestHttpSend::default()) .with_env(OsEnv) .with_command_execute(TokioCommandExecute); let _signer = Signer::new( ctx, DefaultCredentialProvider::new(), RequestSigner::new("s3", "us-east-1"), ); }   Service crates directly — libraries supporting exactly one provider can skip the facade and depend on reqsign-core plus that service crate, letting the application choose context implementations:  [dependencies] reqsign-core = "3" reqsign-aws-v4 = "3"   You are building	UseAn application talking to one or more clouds	facade + default_signer An application with a custom runtime or HTTP stack	facade + custom assembly A library exposing one provider	that service crate directly A WASM target	either, without default-context — see Custom runtimes & WASM

searchDocs.title: The four traits​
searchDocs.content: Trait	Method	Used forFileRead	file_read(path) -> Result<Vec<u8>>	Config files, key files, token files HttpSend	http_send(Request<Bytes>) -> Result<Response<Bytes>>	Metadata endpoints, STS/OIDC exchanges Env	var(key), vars(), home_dir()	Environment-based sources, path expansion CommandExecute	command_execute(cmd, args) -> Result<Output>	CLI-backed sources (e.g. Azure CLI)  (Signatures abbreviated — seedocs.rs/reqsign-core for the precise forms; all futures are MaybeSend.)  The ready-made components the facade uses are ordinary implementations of these traits: TokioFileRead, ReqwestHttpSend, TokioCommandExecute, plus OsEnv from reqsign-core. Mix them freely with your own.

searchDocs.title: Example: an instrumented HTTP sender​
searchDocs.content: use bytes::Bytes; use reqsign::{Context, HttpSend, Result}; use reqsign_http_send_reqwest::ReqwestHttpSend; #[derive(Debug)] struct TracedHttpSend(ReqwestHttpSend); impl HttpSend for TracedHttpSend { async fn http_send(&self, req: http::Request<Bytes>) -> Result<http::Response<Bytes>> { let uri = req.uri().clone(); let started = std::time::Instant::now(); let resp = self.0.http_send(req).await; log::debug!("credential fetch {} took {:?}", uri, started.elapsed()); resp } } let ctx = Context::new().with_http_send(TracedHttpSend(ReqwestHttpSend::default()));   Slots you do not provide stay as no-op stubs that error when used — a credential source that needs a missing capability fails loudly instead of silently returning nothing. The same pattern gives you test doubles: anEnv over a HashMap, an HttpSend over canned responses — seeTesting.

searchDocs.title: WASM​
searchDocs.content: Reqsign's core and a defined subset of providers compile forwasm32-unknown-unknown — signing from browsers, edge runtimes, and plugin sandboxes. CI verifies this exact set on every commit:  reqsign-core, reqsign-aws-core, reqsign-oauth2Providers: AWS SigV4, AWS SigV4a, Azure Storage, GitHub, Aliyun OSS, Aliyun Drive, Backblaze B2, Cloudflare, Tencent COS, Dropbox, OneDrive, Upyun (facade features aws, aws-v4a, azure, github, aliyun,aliyun-drive, b2, cloudflare, tencent, dropbox, onedrive,oauth2, upyun)  GitHub environment, static, and anonymous signing need no JavaScript clock. GitHub CLI discovery requires a CommandExecute adapter and is unavailable in bare WASM runtimes.  Cloudflare environment and static credentials plus header signing need no JavaScript clock.  The provider matrix marks WASM status per provider; treat providers outside this set as unsupported there until the catalog says otherwise.  The OAuth 2.0, Dropbox, Aliyun Drive, and OneDrive paths enable Jiff's jsfeature for wasm32-unknown-unknown. Their public signing and refresh entry points read the clock from a wasm-bindgen JavaScript host such as a browser or Node. A bare WASM runtime without a JavaScript clock can compile the crates but is not a supported runtime; calling Timestamp::now traps there. CI exercises the public Dropbox signing, OAuth2 mock-refresh, Aliyun Drive static and refresh, and OneDrive signing and refresh paths under wasm-bindgen-test in Node.  rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown \ --no-default-features --features aws,azure   Two mechanics keep the crate WASM-clean: no direct filesystem, environment, or process access anywhere outside Context implementations, and trait futures that are MaybeSend — Send on native targets, relaxed on WASM.

searchDocs.title: Providing a browser runtime​
searchDocs.content: There is no filesystem and no OS environment in a browser, so provide what your credential sources actually need — usually just HTTP:  use bytes::Bytes; use reqsign::{Context, HttpSend, Result, Signer}; use reqsign::aws::{RequestSigner, StaticCredentialProvider}; #[derive(Debug)] struct FetchHttpSend; // wraps fetch() via wasm-bindgen impl HttpSend for FetchHttpSend { async fn http_send(&self, req: http::Request<Bytes>) -> Result<http::Response<Bytes>> { todo!("drive the request through fetch()") } } let ctx = Context::new().with_http_send(FetchHttpSend); let signer = Signer::new( ctx, StaticCredentialProvider::new("AKIDEXAMPLE", "example-secret-key"), RequestSigner::new("s3", "us-east-1"), );   Static or externally-injected credentials are the norm on WASM — chains that read files or metadata endpoints have nothing to read in a browser.  Credentials in browsers Anything delivered to a browser is readable by its user. Prefergranted, downscoped credentials or short-lived tokens minted by your backend over long-lived keys.

searchDocs.title: 1. Install​
searchDocs.content: Add the reqsign facade with the feature for each provider you need (features are additive):  cargo add reqsign --features aws cargo add tokio --features full cargo add http anyhow   Feature	Enablesaws	AWS SigV4 (alias of aws-v4) aws-v4a	AWS SigV4a multi-region signing azure	Azure Storage b2	Backblaze B2 Native API cloudflare	Cloudflare API (KV, D1) dropbox	Dropbox github	GitHub.com google	Google Cloud google-credential-access-boundary-client-side	Client-side CAB downscoping (implies google) aliyun	Aliyun OSS aliyun-drive	Aliyun Drive Open Platform huaweicloud	Huawei Cloud OBS http-message-signatures	RFC 9421 request signatures oauth2	Shared OAuth 2.0 refresh-token grant onedrive	OneDrive openstack	OpenStack Keystone oracle	Oracle Cloud tencent	Tencent COS upyun	Upyun volcengine	Volcengine TOS full	Everything above  The default features include default-context, which wires a ready-to-use runtime (Tokio file reading, reqwest HTTP, Tokio command execution), anddefault-crypto, which lets default_context() bind RustCrypto when no process-wide provider is installed. Keep default-context unless you arebringing your own runtime; a custom context must bind a CryptoProvider explicitly. Requires Rust 1.87.0+.

searchDocs.title: 2. Sign your first request​
searchDocs.content: This is the repository's compiled example — CI builds it on every commit:  use anyhow::Result; #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<()> { use reqsign::{aws, default_context}; // Create a default signer for S3 in us-east-1 let ctx = default_context(); let signer = aws::default_signer(ctx, "s3", "us-east-1"); // Build a request let mut req = http::Request::builder() .method(http::Method::GET) .uri("https://s3.amazonaws.com/my-bucket/my-object") .body(()) .unwrap() .into_parts() .0; // Sign the request signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?; // Execute the request would require rebuilding with body // In real usage, you'd use your HTTP client here println!("Request signed successfully!"); Ok(()) }   Three things happen here:  default_context() builds the default runtime context, andaws::default_signer(ctx, "s3", "us-east-1") composes it with AWS's full credential chain — environment variables, shared profiles, SSO, ECS, IMDS, and more. Reuse the same Context across multiple signers by cloning it. See Loading credentials.The request is built with the plain http crate. Reqsign signshttp::request::Parts directly — there is no wrapper client to adopt.signer.sign(&mut req, None).await? mutates the request head in place, adding the Authorization header and companions. PassingSome(duration) instead selects query authentication where the provider supports it — see Presigning.

searchDocs.title: 3. Run it​
searchDocs.content: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIDEXAMPLE \ AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=example-secret \ cargo run   The example signs the request and prints a confirmation; sending it is your HTTP client's job. Any placeholder credentials produce a structurally valid signature — the service rejects them, but the wire format is real.

searchDocs.title: Every provider, one pattern​
searchDocs.content: Swap the entry point and the rest of the code stays the same. Each entry composes that provider's own credential chain — theprovider pages document exactly which sources:  Provider	EntryAWS SigV4	aws::default_signer(ctx, service, region) AWS SigV4a	aws::v4a::default_signer(ctx, service, region_set) Azure Storage	azure::default_signer(ctx) Backblaze B2	b2::default_signer(ctx) Cloudflare	cloudflare::default_signer(ctx) Dropbox	dropbox::default_signer(ctx) GitHub	github::default_signer(ctx) OneDrive	onedrive::default_signer(ctx) Google Cloud	google::default_signer(ctx, service) Aliyun OSS	aliyun::default_signer(ctx, bucket) Aliyun Drive	aliyun_drive::default_signer(ctx) Huawei Cloud OBS	huaweicloud::default_signer(ctx, bucket) HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421)	http_message_signatures::RequestSigner::new(label, components) OpenStack Keystone	openstack::default_signer(ctx) Oracle Cloud	oracle::default_signer(ctx) Tencent COS	tencent::default_signer(ctx) Upyun	upyun::default_signer(ctx, bucket) Volcengine TOS	volcengine::default_signer(ctx, region)  Aliyun Drive has no documented ambient source; replace its default provider with a static access token or refresh-token provider. OneDrive's default chain is also empty; prepend a refresh-token or static provider explicitly.  A default signer is an ordinary Signer: replace any component and keep the rest —  async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { use reqsign::aws::{self, StaticCredentialProvider}; let ctx = reqsign::default_context(); let signer = aws::default_signer(ctx.clone(), "s3", "us-east-1").with_credential_provider( StaticCredentialProvider::new("AKIDEXAMPLE", "example-secret-key"), ); let provider = reqsign::aws::DefaultCredentialProvider::new().push_front( StaticCredentialProvider::new("AKIDEXAMPLE", "example-secret-key"), ); let _custom_chain_signer = aws::default_signer(ctx, "s3", "us-east-1").with_credential_provider(provider); let mut req = http::Request::get("https://s3.amazonaws.com/my-bucket/my-object") .body(())? .into_parts() .0; signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?; assert!(req.headers.contains_key("authorization")); Ok(()) }

searchDocs.title: Where to go next​
searchDocs.content: Wire up credentials your way: Loading credentials.Hand out URLs instead of headers: Presigning.Understand the pieces you just used: Architecture.Check what your provider supports: provider matrix.

searchDocs.title: Use the default chain​
searchDocs.content: Every service crate ships a DefaultCredentialProvider composing that provider's documented default chain — the same sources the official CLIs and SDKs consult, in a documented order. A provider with no documented ambient source has an empty default chain and requires an explicit credential provider. Each provider page lists its exact sources.  use reqsign::aws::DefaultCredentialProvider; // The documented default chain for AWS: // env → profiles (including assume-role chains) → SSO → OIDC → process → ECS → IMDS let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::new();   Every DefaultCredentialProvider exposes the same four entry points:  DefaultCredentialProvider::new(); // the documented default chain DefaultCredentialProvider::builder(); // default slots, then adjust DefaultCredentialProvider::with_chain(chain); // bypass defaults entirely DefaultCredentialProvider::new().push_front(provider); // prepend a high-priority source

searchDocs.title: Adjust the chain​
searchDocs.content: The builder pre-populates the default slots. Each slot has exactly two methods — one to replace it, one to remove it:  use reqsign::aws::{DefaultCredentialProvider, EnvCredentialProvider}; // Replace the env slot, drop IMDS, keep everything else as documented. let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::builder() .env(EnvCredentialProvider::new()) .no_imds() .build();   There are no configure_* or disable_*(bool) methods by design: a removed slot stays removed, and every slot is controlled by one positive and one removal method.

searchDocs.title: IMDSv1 fallback​
searchDocs.content: The AWS IMDS provider uses IMDSv2 by default. To allow IMDSv1 when the IMDSv2 token request returns HTTP 403, 404, or 405, opt in on the IMDS slot:  use reqsign::aws::{DefaultCredentialProvider, IMDSv2CredentialProvider}; let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::builder() .imds(IMDSv2CredentialProvider::new().with_imdsv1_fallback()) .build();   Other token, transport, metadata, role, and credential failures are returned without falling back. Enable this only for instances where IMDSv2 is unavailable.

searchDocs.title: Fixed credentials​
searchDocs.content: When the credential is decided elsewhere — tests, WASM, a control plane that injects keys — skip chains entirely:  use reqsign::aws::{self, StaticCredentialProvider}; let ctx = reqsign::default_context(); let signer = aws::default_signer(ctx.clone(), "s3", "us-east-1").with_credential_provider( StaticCredentialProvider::new("AKIDEXAMPLE", "example-secret-key"), );   Replacing a signer's context or credential provider clears its credential cache, so a credential from the old configuration is never reused with the new one.

searchDocs.title: Implement your own source​
searchDocs.content: When credentials come from somewhere Reqsign doesn't know — a secret manager, a sidecar, an in-house vault — implement ProvideCredential:  use bytes::Bytes; use reqsign::{Context, ProvideCredential, Result}; use reqsign::aws::Credential; #[derive(Debug)] struct VaultCredentialProvider { endpoint: String, } impl ProvideCredential for VaultCredentialProvider { type Credential = Credential; async fn provide_credential(&self, ctx: &Context) -> Result<Option<Self::Credential>> { // Use the Context for I/O so your provider stays runtime-agnostic // and testable — here, an HTTP call through ctx. let req = http::Request::get(&self.endpoint).body(Bytes::new())?; let resp = ctx.http_send(req).await?; // Return Ok(None) when this source has nothing to offer, // so a chain can continue to the next provider. if resp.status() == http::StatusCode::NOT_FOUND { return Ok(None); } let credential = parse_vault_response(resp.body())?; Ok(Some(credential)) } }   The return-value protocol is what makes chains compose: Ok(Some(_))resolves and Ok(None) passes to the next source. ProvideCredentialChainalso logs Err(_) and continues: a failing custom source can fall back to profiles, metadata, or another configured identity. If all sources fail or return None, the chain returns Ok(None).  Report "not configured" as None and real failures as errors. When failure must stop credential resolution, install your provider directly on the signer or implement a chain with that policy; prepending a provider does not enforce it. A provider installed directly has its errors propagated by Signer. SeeArchitecture § ProvideCredential.

searchDocs.title: Plug it in​
searchDocs.content: Highest priority in front of the default chain:  use reqsign::aws::DefaultCredentialProvider; let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::new().push_front(VaultCredentialProvider { endpoint: "http://127.0.0.1:8200/v1/aws/creds/my-role".into(), });   Or a fully explicit chain that bypasses the defaults:  use reqsign::ProvideCredentialChain; let chain = ProvideCredentialChain::new() .push(VaultCredentialProvider { endpoint }) .push(EnvCredentialProvider::new()); let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::with_chain(chain);   Then hand it to a default signer (.with_credential_provider(provider)) or a custom Signer::new.

searchDocs.title: Freshness​
searchDocs.content: The credential type you return implements SigningCredential; set its expiration socaching refreshes it on time. Credentials without an expiration are cached by the signer until its credential provider is replaced. Replacing the signer's Context also clears the signer's credential cache.

searchDocs.title: The operations​
searchDocs.content: Provider	Operation	Scopes toAWS SigV4	S3 Access Grants (GetDataAccess)	A registered grant: location, prefix, permission AWS SigV4	S3 Express Session (CreateSession)	One directory bucket, read-only or read-write Azure Storage	User delegation SAS	Container/blob, permissions, validity window Google Cloud	Credential Access Boundary (server-side)	Buckets/prefixes via an STS exchange Google Cloud	Credential Access Boundary (client-side)	Same, derived locally without an STS round-trip  Each operation is listed with source references on itsprovider page.

searchDocs.title: Walkthrough: S3 Express session credentials​
searchDocs.content: The same dependencies as Getting Started suffice. This example uses the default context for environment, file, and HTTP access:  use reqsign::aws::{ DefaultCredentialProvider, S3ExpressSessionConfig, S3ExpressSessionGrant, S3ExpressSessionGranter, S3ExpressSessionMode, }; use reqsign::{Granter, default_context}; #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let config = S3ExpressSessionConfig::from_bucket("my-bucket--usw2-az1--x-s3", "us-west-2")?; let grant = S3ExpressSessionGrant::new(S3ExpressSessionMode::ReadOnly); let granter = Granter::new( default_context(), DefaultCredentialProvider::new(), S3ExpressSessionGranter::new(config, grant), ); let scoped = granter.grant(None).await?; // Keep the entire credential, including expires_in, when passing it on. assert!(scoped.expires_in.is_some()); Ok(()) }

searchDocs.title: Signing with automatically refreshed sessions​
searchDocs.content: For a long-lived signer, use S3ExpressSessionProvider. It performs the same CreateSession exchange when credentials are needed, preserves their expiration, and lets Signer refresh the session. S3 Express uses the s3express signing service and the directory bucket's zonal endpoint:  use reqsign::aws::{ self, DefaultCredentialProvider, S3ExpressSessionGrant, S3ExpressSessionMode, S3ExpressSessionProvider, }; use reqsign::default_context; #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let provider = S3ExpressSessionProvider::new( "my-bucket--usw2-az1--x-s3", DefaultCredentialProvider::new(), ) .with_region("us-west-2") .with_grant(S3ExpressSessionGrant::new(S3ExpressSessionMode::ReadOnly)); let signer = aws::default_signer(default_context(), "s3express", "us-west-2") .with_credential_provider(provider); let mut req = http::Request::get( "https://my-bucket--usw2-az1--x-s3.s3express-usw2-az1.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/object", ) .body(())? .into_parts() .0; // The signer caches the session with its expiration and refreshes as needed. signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?; Ok(()) }   When passing a manually granted credential to another component, retain the entire credential, including expires_in. Reconstructing it with AWS'sStaticCredentialProvider loses the expiration and automatic refresh behavior. Keep granted keys and session tokens out of logs.

searchDocs.title: Semantics to rely on​
searchDocs.content: The source credential is cached and revalidated per grant; the granted result owns independent material and never aliases the cache.expires_in requests a validity window where the operation supports one; the operation's own maximum applies.Errors returned by the configured source or grant operation propagate without retry or reuse of a stale cached source. A source configured as a credential chain can still fall back between its providers.  Credential fields and types are provider-specific — seedocs.rs for the exact API.

searchDocs.title: Produce a presigned URL​
searchDocs.content: use reqsign::{aws, default_context}; use std::time::Duration; #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> { let ctx = default_context(); let signer = aws::default_signer(ctx, "s3", "us-east-1"); let mut req = http::Request::get("https://s3.amazonaws.com/my-bucket/report.csv") .body(())? .into_parts() .0; signer .sign(&mut req, Some(Duration::from_secs(3600))) .await?; // Share req.uri over a trusted channel; it contains authentication material. assert!(req.uri.query().is_some()); Ok(()) }   For AWS this produces X-Amz-Algorithm, X-Amz-Credential,X-Amz-Expires, X-Amz-Signature, and companions in the query string. Other providers use their own parameter sets; the shape of the call is identical.  OpenStack Swift TempURL is the exception: it signs with a separate account or container key rather than the Keystone credential. Usereqsign::openstack::TempUrlSigner instead of the default signer; see theOpenStack provider for the key, algorithm, and canonical-path contract.

searchDocs.title: expires_in is service-specific​
searchDocs.content: Passing Some(duration) does not universally mean "presign" — the configured service signer and credential type determine how the duration is interpreted:  AWS SigV4/SigV4a, Aliyun OSS, Tencent COS, Volcengine TOS, Google Cloud Storage, and Huawei Cloud OBS select query authentication with that validity window.Azure Storage SAS credentials authenticate through the query string by nature; shared keys and bearer tokens sign headers.Oracle Cloud bounds credential validity but produces no query authentication — header signing is its only mode.Cloudflare has no query authentication at all, so it rejects expires_ininstead of ignoring it.  The provider matrix carries the authoritative header/query flags, and theexpiration contractstates the exact semantics.

searchDocs.title: Before you ship one​
searchDocs.content: The method and URI are part of the signature. A URL presigned forGET /report.csv authorizes exactly that — not PUT, not another key.Credential validity must cover the window. The signer refreshes a cached credential that would expire before expires_in elapses, and errors if no credential can cover the window — a URL that dies early is a bug, not a surprise. SeeCredential freshness.Anyone with the URL is authorized. Treat presigned URLs as secrets with a TTL: transmit over TLS, scope tightly, keep windows short.Never re-encode a presigned URI. The signature covers the provider-defined wire representation; a second encoding pass breaks it. SeeWire-ready URIs.Tighter blast radius: grant a downscoped credential first and presign with that.

searchDocs.title: Signing tests with fixed credentials​
searchDocs.content: Use fixed credentials to check signing without credential-source I/O. Signing still uses the current time, so this example checks the authentication header rather than asserting a timestamp-dependent signature:  use reqsign::{Context, RustCryptoProvider, Signer}; use reqsign::aws::{RequestSigner, StaticCredentialProvider}; let signer = Signer::new( // No I/O needed with static credentials; bind crypto locally. Context::new().with_crypto(RustCryptoProvider::new()), StaticCredentialProvider::new("AKIDEXAMPLE", "example-secret-key"), RequestSigner::new("s3", "us-east-1"), ); let mut req = http::Request::builder() .method(http::Method::GET) .uri("https://s3.amazonaws.com/test-bucket/test-object") .body(())? .into_parts() .0; signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?; assert!(req.headers.contains_key("authorization"));   Use obviously fake material (AKIDEXAMPLE) in fixtures — never real keys, not even expired ones.

searchDocs.title: Mocking the environment​
searchDocs.content: Credential chains read env vars and files through Context, so tests inject them without process-global mutation:  use reqsign::{Context, Env}; #[derive(Debug)] struct StaticEnv(std::collections::HashMap<String, String>); impl Env for StaticEnv { fn var(&self, key: &str) -> Option<String> { self.0.get(key).cloned() } // ...remaining methods delegate similarly } let ctx = Context::new().with_env(StaticEnv( [("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID".into(), "AKIDEXAMPLE".into()), ("AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY".into(), "example-secret-key".into())] .into(), ));   The same pattern applies to HttpSend (canned metadata/STS responses) andFileRead (in-memory profiles). This is exactly how the repository tests IMDS, ECS, SSO, and OIDC flows against local mock servers underservices/aws-v4/tests/mocks.

searchDocs.title: Integration tests against real services​
searchDocs.content: Per-service integration suites live under services/<name>/tests/ and stay skipped unless their REQSIGN_* environment variables opt in — see each suite's README for the exact gate. CI wires secrets for them; locally you can run the mock-backed tests with plain cargo test.

searchDocs.title: What "supported" means​
searchDocs.content: For each provider, the detail page states precisely:  Service scope — which APIs the signer produces valid signatures for.Signing schemes — the exact protocols implemented (e.g. SigV4, Shared Key, OSS V4).Credential sources — which loading mechanisms the default chain composes.Request authentication — whether header signing, query authentication, or both are available.Credential granting — explicit downscoping operations, if any.WASM status — whether CI verifies the provider forwasm32-unknown-unknown.Test coverage — how the claims are exercised (mock servers, fixtures, gated live tests).  Reqsign does not claim to support "every cloud" or every service of any cloud — only what this catalog declares and traces to source.

searchDocs.title: Credentials​
searchDocs.content: Aliyun Drive Open Platform documents OAuth authorization and its token endpoint, but no CLI, SDK, environment-variable, or local-file credential discovery contract. Reqsign therefore does not invent an ambient source. UseStaticCredentialProvider for a caller-managed access token, orRefreshCredentialProvider for a confidential-client refresh token.  An explicit provider fails closed: an invalid token or refresh configuration returns an error instead of silently switching to a different identity.

searchDocs.title: Refresh-token exchange​
searchDocs.content: Aliyun Drive uses OAuth 2.0 authorization but not the RFC 6749 form-encoded refresh request. The provider sends a vendor-specific JSON body:  POST https://openapi.alipan.com/oauth/access_token Content-Type: application/json User-Agent: reqsign-aliyun-drive/<version> {"client_id":"...","client_secret":"...","grant_type":"refresh_token","refresh_token":"..."}   All three confidential-client credentials are required. Aliyun Drive's official PKCE public-client flow returns a 30-day access token without a refresh token, so public clients use StaticCredentialProvider with that access token, optionally with its absolute expiration. The endpoint requires a non-emptyUser-Agent. Use with_token_endpoint only to select another explicitly trusted HTTPS endpoint for the same confidential-client protocol.  A successful response returns access_token, token_type, expires_in, and a new single-use refresh_token. The provider keeps only the latest refresh token in memory. Clones share that state and exchanges are serialized, so concurrent callers use the latest rotated token. A successful, parseable response commits a non-empty rotated token even when the accompanying access token or expiry is unusable, because the previous refresh token was consumed. Tokens are never persisted, and Reqsign exposes no getter or persistence callback.reqsign::Signer owns access-token caching and refresh on expiry.  After a successful refresh, the initially configured refresh token may already have been consumed. Restarting with that original value can therefore fail. Restart with a fresh authorized grant, or let the application manage and persist its own refresh exchange and supply the resulting access token throughStaticCredentialProvider.  use reqsign::{Signer, aliyun_drive, default_context}; let provider = aliyun_drive::RefreshCredentialProvider::new( "client-id", "client-secret", "refresh-token", )?; let signer = Signer::new(default_context(), provider, aliyun_drive::RequestSigner);

searchDocs.title: Request behavior​
searchDocs.content: RequestSigner inserts a sensitive Authorization: Bearer header and leaves the URI and every other header unchanged. Drive IDs, file paths, upload URLs, request bodies, and the storage API requests stay with the caller. The service has no query authentication, so signing rejects expires_in.  The first-party storage API also requires a caller-supplied User-Agent; the signer does not add or replace it. The refresh request sets its ownUser-Agent because the token endpoint requires one.  The caller owns the HTTP client and its redirect policy. Do not forward the signed Authorization header to a different host.

searchDocs.title: Resource identifiers stay in the request​
searchDocs.content: The account, database, and namespace identifiers are part of the request URL rather than the credential:  KV /accounts/<account_id>/storage/kv/namespaces/<namespace_id>/values/<key> D1 /accounts/<account_id>/d1/database/<database_id>/query   They stay with the code that builds the request, so one credential signs for every account, database, and namespace the token is scoped to. Reqsign does not build the business URL, choose the HTTP method, or touch the request body: keep the multipart Content-Type for KV writes and the JSON body for D1 queries in the caller.

searchDocs.title: Credential discovery​
searchDocs.content: The default chain reads CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN through Context environment access. That is the variable Wrangler and Cloudflare's official SDKs use for non-interactive authentication. There is no other default source.  Cloudflare's global API key is not an API token source: it authenticates withX-Auth-Key and X-Auth-Email instead of a bearer token, soCLOUDFLARE_API_KEY and CLOUDFLARE_EMAIL are not read. Supply a custom provider when a request really needs that authentication.  CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID is not read either; it selects a resource in the URL, not an identity.  The configured sources fail closed. A present but unusableCLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, or an invalid prepended or static provider, fails signing instead of silently selecting a different identity. An absent token yields no credential, and signing then reports CredentialInvalid.

searchDocs.title: Request behavior​
searchDocs.content: RequestSigner inserts a sensitive Authorization header and leaves the URI and every other header unchanged. The Cloudflare API has no query authentication, so signing rejects expires_in.  Cloudflare assigns each token its permissions and optional expiry when the token is created; neither is readable from the token. Reqsign does not track that expiry, and signing writes no protocol time, so signing has no clock dependency. A token that Cloudflare has expired fails at the API, so rotate it with the mechanism your deployment already uses.  The caller owns the HTTP client and its redirect policy. Do not forward the signed Authorization header to a different host.

searchDocs.title: Get started​
searchDocs.content: cargo add reqsign --features github   use reqsign::{default_context, github}; // GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN, then the GitHub CLI, then anonymous public access. let ctx = default_context(); let signer = github::default_signer(ctx); let mut req = http::Request::builder() .method(http::Method::GET) .uri("https://api.github.com/repos/apache/reqsign/contents/README.md") .header("user-agent", "my-application") .header("x-github-api-version", "2022-11-28") .body(())? .into_parts() .0; // Sign in place, then send with the HTTP client you already use. signer.sign(&mut req, None).await?;   The default chain reads GH_TOKEN before GITHUB_TOKEN. If neither is set and the context has a CommandExecute adapter, it resolves the active stored account with gh config get user --host github.com, then reads that account's token withgh auth token --hostname github.com --user <user> --no-refresh. The explicit user prevents GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN in the child process environment from shadowing the stored credential; safe stored-token discovery requires GitHub CLI 2.40.0 or newer. The commands run directly, never through a shell; the explicit host keeps discovery independent of GH_HOST and local Git remotes; and Reqsign does not parse the CLI's configuration files.  --no-refresh keeps discovery read-only on GitHub CLI 2.103.0 and newer. Older supported versions do not refresh when printing a stored token, so the provider retries without the flag only after the CLI reports that specific flag as unknown. If the stored token has expired, run gh auth refresh, then recreate the signer so it loads the new token.  The default slots stop at the first error instead of silently selecting a different identity. A malformed environment token, malformed or failed stored-token discovery, or an invalid prepended or static provider fails signing. Only an absent credential reaches anonymous access.  With no token, the chain ends with anonymous access. Signing with an anonymous credential removes any existing Authorization header and leaves other headers and the URI unchanged, so a reused request cannot carry stale authentication material. Anonymous requests can read public resources and are subject to GitHub's 60-requests-per-hour unauthenticated rate limit. searchDocs.title: Request behavior​
searchDocs.content: RequestSigner adds a sensitive Authorization: Bearer header for a token credential and removes any existing Authorization header for an explicit anonymous credential. GitHub has no query authentication, so signing rejects expires_in. GitHub credentials in this crate carry no expiration and signing writes no protocol time, so signing has no clock dependency.

searchDocs.title: Host and scope​
searchDocs.content: The built-in providers discover GitHub.com credentials only. The signer does not restrict the request host, so caller-supplied credentials may be used with another GitHub host. GitHub assigns each token's host and its OAuth scopes or fine-grained repository permissions. Reqsign neither requests nor inspects them, and it does not implement GitHub App installation-token exchange.  The caller owns the HTTP client and its redirect policy. searchDocs.title: Scope​
searchDocs.content: This first version signs request heads with HMAC-SHA256 or RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 SHA-256. It supports ordinary request fields and the@method, @target-uri, @authority, @scheme, @path, and @queryderived components. Percent escapes, query order, and repeated query parameters are preserved.  The signer requires an absolute HTTP or HTTPS URI. @target-uri is rebuilt from the scheme, the authority exactly as written, and the origin-form path/query, with an empty path normalized to /. A present Host header must be unique and byte-identical to the URI authority; case-only or explicit/default-port differences are rejected because an HTTP/1.1 origin-form receiver could reconstruct a different target URI. Origin-form request targets without an absolute URI are not supported.  Verification, response signing, multiple signatures in one call, component parameters, @request-target, and body I/O are out of scope. To cover a body, compute a Content-Digest before signing and include it in the component list.  HMAC uses raw shared-key bytes. RSA accepts unencrypted PKCS#1 or PKCS#8 PEM and uses the context's CryptoProvider. The RustCrypto provider supports RSA on native targets but returns ConfigInvalid for it on wasm32-unknown-unknown. The HMAC path runs on wasm32-unknown-unknown when hosted by a JavaScript runtime through wasm-bindgen, such as a browser or Node. Jiff reads the clock from that host; a bare WASM runtime without a JavaScript clock is unsupported.

searchDocs.title: Refresh tokens​
searchDocs.content: The authorization request must include offline_access to receive a refresh token, plus the Microsoft Graph scope your access needs. Files.ReadWrite is the least privileged delegated permission that lets the app read, create, update, and delete the signed-in user's files, and Files.Read is the read-only alternative. Reqsign refreshes throughhttps://login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/v2.0/token.  A public client — desktop, mobile, browserless, or client-side app — cannot store an application secret, so the exchange sends none:  use reqsign::{default_context, onedrive::default_signer}; use reqsign::onedrive::{DefaultCredentialProvider, RefreshCredentialProvider}; let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::new() .push_front(RefreshCredentialProvider::new("client-id", "refresh-token")?); let signer = default_signer(default_context()).with_credential_provider(provider);   A confidential client — web app, web API, or daemon that keeps the secret on the server side — adds it to the same form-body exchange:  use reqsign::{default_context, onedrive::default_signer}; use reqsign::onedrive::{DefaultCredentialProvider, RefreshCredentialProvider}; let provider = DefaultCredentialProvider::new().push_front( RefreshCredentialProvider::builder("client-id", "refresh-token") .client_secret("client-secret") .build()?, ); let signer = default_signer(default_context()).with_credential_provider(provider);   Microsoft returns a new refresh token with every successful exchange and documents that the client must discard the previous one. A provider keeps only the latest refresh token in memory, clones share it, and exchanges are serialized, so concurrent signing never races two exchanges with the same token. Reqsign never writes refresh tokens to disk; a refresh token lost with the process must be obtained again through the authorization flow.  A Microsoft Graph token response carries expires_in. A successful exchange that omits it, or whose token is already expired, is rejected rather than cached as a token with an unknown lifetime; the returned refresh token from that response is still committed for the next exchange. Access-token caching and proactive refresh belong to Signer.

searchDocs.title: Tenant, scope, and endpoint​
searchDocs.content: The default token endpoint is the global Microsoft Entra v2.0 endpoint for thecommon tenant. Microsoft documents common, organizations, consumers, or a tenant identifier such as a domain name or GUID; select one with .tenant:  use reqsign::onedrive::RefreshCredentialProvider; let provider = RefreshCredentialProvider::builder("client-id", "refresh-token") .tenant("contoso.onmicrosoft.com") .build()?;   By default the exchange omits scope, which keeps the new access token limited to what the original grant received. To repeat the scope explicitly, use.scope("offline_access Files.ReadWrite"); Microsoft requires the value to be equivalent to or a subset of the original grant. Requesting a broader scope than the user consented to fails the exchange.  National clouds publish their own Microsoft Entra authentication endpoints, for example https://login.microsoftonline.us for Microsoft Entra ID for US Government and https://login.partner.microsoftonline.cn for Microsoft Entra China. Replace the whole endpoint in those clouds; it must be HTTPS:  use reqsign::onedrive::RefreshCredentialProvider; let provider = RefreshCredentialProvider::builder("client-id", "refresh-token") .token_endpoint("https://login.microsoftonline.us/common/oauth2/v2.0/token") .build()?;

WithoutOS_AUTH_TOKEN, the chain authenticates against the Keystone v3 identity API with OS_AUTH_URL, OS_USERNAME, and OS_PASSWORD. searchDocs.title: Swift TempURL​
searchDocs.content: TempURL presigning is separate from X-Auth-Token request signing. It uses the account or container key configured through X-Account-Meta-Temp-URL-Key orX-Container-Meta-Temp-URL-Key; it never uses a Keystone identity token as the key.  use std::time::Duration; use reqsign::{default_context, openstack}; let ctx = default_context(); let signer = openstack::TempUrlSigner::new("account-tempurl-key") .with_algorithm(openstack::TempUrlHashAlgorithm::Sha256); let uri = "https://swift.example.com/v1/AUTH_test/container/object" .parse()?; let presigned = signer.presign( &ctx, &http::Method::GET, &uri, Duration::from_secs(3600), )?;   The signature covers the method, the absolute expiration time, and the object path after decoding its percent escapes once, matching Swift's decoded request path. The outgoing URI keeps the caller's encoded path and query bytes and order. Existing non-auth query parameters are preserved, and a pre-existing TempURL authentication parameter is rejected even when its name is percent-encoded.  The provider always emits sha1:, sha256:, or sha512: HMAC tags with standard Base64 digests; SHA-256 is the default. Current Swift accepts this form, and the selected digest must be in the deployment'stempurl.allowed_digests. Current middleware defaults to all three, with SHA-1 deprecated, and deployments may restrict the list. A capability that exposestempurl without allowed_digests belongs to the legacy raw-hex-only boundary, such as Swift 2.16, and is not supported even with SHA-1 selected. SHA-512 requires a CryptoProvider that implements hmac_sha512. Prefix-based and IP-restricted TempURLs are not provided.  Swift rebuilds the downstream query string from its recognized TempURL fields and removes or filters incoming headers according to the deployment configuration. This client preserves the caller's outgoing query and headers, but arbitrary query components or headers are not guaranteed to reach the storage service through a TempURL.

searchDocs.title: Wire-ready URIs​
searchDocs.content: The contract: sign takes a wire-ready request head. The URI you pass is the URI that goes on the wire — built-in signers require an authority and expect path and query data to be percent-encoded exactly once before the call. Signing does not perform general-purpose URI encoding for the caller.  Signature protocols canonicalize the URI (SigV4 builds its canonical request from the encoded path and sorted query). If the signer re-encoded your input, an already-encoded %2F would double-encode while a raw space got "helpfully" fixed — and the signed bytes would depend on who encoded last. Exactly-once encoding, owned by the caller, removes the ambiguity: what you signed is what you send.  Swift TempURL is a provider-specific exception. Its separate presign entry point keeps the caller's encoded path and query bytes in the outgoing URI, but uses the path after one percent-decoding step for the HMAC input, matching the decoded request path Swift verifies.  // Object key: "reports/2026 Q1.csv" — encode once when building the URI: let uri = "https://s3.amazonaws.com/my-bucket/reports/2026%20Q1.csv";   Rules of thumb: encode path segments and query values once, when constructing the URI; never pass a decoded "pretty" URI expecting a fix-up; never re-encode after signing (for presigned URLs this breaks the signature); relative URIs are not signable. Some service crates export percent-encoding helpers tuned to their provider's canonicalization (for example reqsign-volcengine-tos's percent_encode_path).

searchDocs.title: Atomic request mutation​
searchDocs.content: The contract: if credential loading or request signing returns an error, the request is unchanged. On success, only req.uri and req.headersmay change; the method, version, and extensions retain their input values.  match signer.sign(&mut req, None).await { Ok(()) => { /* req is signed: uri and/or headers updated, nothing else */ } Err(e) => { /* req is byte-for-byte what you built */ } }   Without atomicity, an error path could leave a half-signed request — anAuthorization header from one attempt, query parameters from another — forcing callers to rebuild requests defensively around every failure. With it: retries reuse the original request as-is, fallback signing is safe, and a request never carries remnants of a signature that was not fully produced. The guarantee covers the request head; bodies are never touched.

searchDocs.title: Credential freshness​
searchDocs.content: The contract: a cached credential is reused only when it is fresh according to SigningCredential::is_valid and usable through the operation's deadline (required_valid_until). A freshly loaded credential only needs to satisfy the exact operation deadline. Provider errors are returned without internal retry and without falling back to the previously cached credential.  The two validity checks have different jobs — is_valid() answers thecaching question and may include a proactive refresh window;is_valid_at(ts) answers the operation question with no buffers (seeArchitecture). Deadlines come from the operation: essentially "now" for header signing, the full window for a presigned URL — so a credential expiring in five minutes triggers a refresh rather than producing a URL that dies early.

searchDocs.title: Expiration semantics​
searchDocs.content: The contract: expires_in is a service-specific validity input. It does not universally select query authentication — the configured service signer and credential type determine how the duration is interpreted.  Interpretation	ProvidersSelects query authentication with that validity window	AWS SigV4/SigV4a, Aliyun OSS, Tencent COS, Volcengine TOS, Google Cloud Storage (V4 signed URLs), Huawei Cloud OBS Bounds credential validity; header signing regardless	Oracle Cloud Ignored; header signing always uses the current Date	Upyun Rejected; header authentication only	Aliyun Drive, Cloudflare Requests a granted credential's validity window	Granting operations (subject to the operation's own maximum)  Whatever the provider does with it, one obligation is universal: the credential used must remain usable for the full window — the signer refreshes or errors rather than producing an artifact that dies early. And three things it never means: it never shortens a credential's own lifetime; it never overrides a provider-side maximum (S3 presign caps at 7 days — exceeding a cap is a provider-side error, not silent truncation); and None never means "no expiry" for the artifact (header signatures still embed timestamps with provider-defined validity).

searchDocs.title: Secret redaction​
searchDocs.content: The contract: formatting Reqsign types with Debug does not reveal secret material. Credential types implement Debug by hand, wrapping sensitive fields in a Redact helper; composite types like Signer print structure, not contents. Non-sensitive metadata (like expiration) prints normally so logs stay useful.  log::debug!("loaded: {credential:?}"); // Credential { access_key_id: Redacted, secret_access_key: Redacted, ... }   Redaction covers accidental leaks — {:?} in a log line, a panic message, an error chain. It cannot protect secrets you extract on purpose: accessor methods return real values, and a signed request's Authorization header or presigned URI contains derived authentication material — log a presigned URI and you have logged a usable capability. Redact at your logging layer, and give custom ProvideCredential implementations a manual Debug over redacted fields too. Report suspected leaks through theASF security process, never the public issue tracker.

searchDocs.title: Errors and retries​
searchDocs.content: The contract: The signer and granter propagate errors returned by their configured provider; you own retries. sign andgrant perform no internal retries, no fallback signers, and no silent reuse of stale credentials. Combined with atomic mutation, any error leaves the request head unchanged — free to retry, reroute, or fail. This does not prevent a ProvideCredentialChain from trying later sources after individual provider errors; see Loading credentials.  reqsign_core::Error carries an ErrorKind designed for retry decisions:  Kind	Meaning	Sensible defaultCredentialInvalid	Credential missing, expired, or unusable	Refresh source, then retry PermissionDenied	Authenticated but not authorized	Do not retry ConfigInvalid	Malformed profile/config input	Fix configuration; do not retry RequestInvalid	The request cannot be signed as given	Fix the request; do not retry RateLimited	A credential endpoint throttled us	Retry with backoff Unexpected	Transient or unclassified failure	Retry with backoff, bounded  Errors preserve their source chain (std::error::Error::source), so transport details from a metadata fetch or STS exchange stay inspectable.  Why no built-in retry: Reqsign sits inside clients that already have retry policies — an HTTP middleware, a storage layer, a job runner. A second, inner retry loop multiplies attempts invisibly and turns rate limits into storms. Most callers simply propagate signing errors to the layer that already retries requests.

searchDocs.title: Versioning​
searchDocs.content: Reqsign publishes many crates on four tracks:  Track	Crates	SchemeCore + existing services	reqsign-core, reqsign-aws-core, every existing reqsign-<provider> service crate, reqsign-file-read-tokio, reqsign-command-execute-tokio	Lockstep major (currently 3.x) New provider and shared crates	reqsign-b2, reqsign-oauth2, reqsign-dropbox, reqsign-aliyun-drive, reqsign-github, reqsign-cloudflare, reqsign-onedrive, and later crates introduced after the lockstep line	Independent major, starting at 1.0.0 Reqwest adapter	reqsign-http-send-reqwest	Independent major (currently 4.x), so reqwest major bumps do not force a core major Facade	reqsign	Independent (currently 0.20.x)  Lockstep means any 3.x established service crate composes with any 3.xcore. New provider and shared crates start at 1.0.0 and depend on the current core major, so a 1.x crate composes with 3.x core. Mixing core majors fails to compile — the trait definitions are the compatibility boundary, and Cargo enforces it.  Applications should depend on the facade and let it pin compatible components; libraries should depend on reqsign-core plus their service crates with major-only bounds, leaving context implementations to the application:  # Application: reqsign = { version = "0.20", features = ["aws"] } # Library: reqsign-core = "3" reqsign-aws-v4 = "3"   Every release ships as an ASF source release plus crates.io packages — seeDownload. Release notes and migration steps for breaking majors are published with eachGitHub release.

searchDocs.title: Targets​
searchDocs.content: Rust version. The workspace declares rust-version = "1.87.0" — the minimum supported Rust. The RustCrypto backend's rsa 0.10 dependency requires this version. CI tracks stable; MSRV bumps are treated as observable changes, not patch-level noise.  Native. Reqsign is pure Rust with no C dependencies of its own; CI exercises Linux, macOS, and Windows. The default context components (Tokio file reading and command execution, reqwest HTTP) run wherever those crates do.  WASM. wasm32-unknown-unknown is a supported, CI-verified target for a defined subset: reqsign-core, reqsign-aws-core, and the AWS SigV4, AWS SigV4a, Azure Storage, GitHub, Aliyun OSS, Aliyun Drive, Backblaze B2, Cloudflare, Tencent COS, Dropbox, OneDrive, and Upyun providers. The sharedreqsign-oauth2 crate and the oauth2 facade feature are checked in the same subset. Cloudflare environment and static credentials plus header signing work without a JavaScript clock. GitHub environment, static, and anonymous signing work without a JavaScript clock; GitHub CLI discovery needs aCommandExecute adapter and is unavailable in bare WASM runtimes. Dropbox, OAuth2, Aliyun Drive, and OneDrive runtime signing or refresh additionally requires a wasm-bindgen JavaScript host for the clock; see theCustom runtimes & WASM guide. Theprovider matrix is the authoritative per-provider status.  Async runtimes. reqsign-core is runtime-agnostic — nothing in core assumes Tokio. Runtime coupling lives only in the optional context crates; swap them to run elsewhere.
